outcomes.text: You help compare the measures before the grain is divided. The neighbors thank you and keep the shares separate.

choices.text: Keep buying for your own household

outcomes.text: You leave the shared purchase to the neighbors and keep to your usual food arrangement.

events.title: A hinge still needs fitting
events.text: You have promised to fit a wooden hinge for someone nearby. Another task has used most of the time you set aside.

choices.text: Finish the fitting before going home

outcomes.text: You check the hinge against the opening and finish it before leaving. The extra work makes for a late meal.

choices.text: Explain the delay and agree on another time

outcomes.text: You tell the household before they start waiting for you. They agree to the new time.

choices.text: Ask another worker to finish it

outcomes.text: Another worker can finish the fitting. You pass over your measurements and leave the rest of the task to them.

events.title: A payment arrives late
events.text: Someone who owes you 10 drachmas for a small job says they cannot pay the whole amount today.

choices.text: Accept 5 drachmas and leave the rest for later

outcomes.text: They pay 5 drachmas now. You agree that the remaining amount is still owed.

choices.text: Accept useful household goods instead

outcomes.text: You agree on goods your household needs and settle the payment that way. The next meal takes less preparation.

choices.text: Agree on a later collection day

outcomes.text: You leave without payment and agree when to return. You keep a note of the amount so there is no dispute later.

events.title: Different plans for the visit
events.text: You and the person you are courting have made different plans for the same free afternoon.

choices.text: Join the visit they planned

outcomes.text: You go with their plan and help carry something for the visit. You have time to talk on the return walk.

choices.text: Choose another time together

outcomes.text: You compare the errands each of you must finish and find a time that works for both.

choices.text: Keep your own plan this time

outcomes.text: You keep the afternoon for your own plans. The other person is disappointed, but the disagreement stays small.

events.title: Two uses for the same coins
events.text: You and your spouse disagree about whether spare cash should go toward supplies or a shared meal with relatives.

choices.text: Check the household supplies together

outcomes.text: You go through what is left before deciding. The discussion settles which purchases can wait.

choices.text: Spend 5 drachmas on a smaller shared meal

outcomes.text: You agree on a smaller meal and spend 5 drachmas. There is still time to talk after the visitors arrive.

choices.text: Leave the coins untouched for now

outcomes.text: You postpone the purchase and the meal. The money stays available, though the decision still needs to be made.

events.title: A child asks about letters
events.text: One of your children asks you to explain marks on a delivered message. You have a little time before the next task.

choices.text: Ask a familiar reader to explain them

outcomes.text: A reader explains a few marks with you both listening. The child repeats them on the way home.

choices.text: Show the child the marks you know

outcomes.text: You explain the marks you recognize and leave the unfamiliar ones for someone who knows more.

choices.text: Finish the household task first

outcomes.text: You put the message somewhere safe and finish the task. The child goes back to playing nearby.

events.title: A child wants to help with work
events.text: One of your children asks for a task while you are arranging materials. There are safe small jobs, but they will need watching.

choices.text: Let the child sort harmless scraps nearby

outcomes.text: You set aside small safe pieces to sort and keep the tools out of reach. You check the piles together when the child finishes.

choices.text: Explain the task without having them do it

outcomes.text: You show the finished pieces and explain what each part does. The child asks more questions than you expected.

choices.text: Keep the work area clear today

outcomes.text: You explain that the task needs your full attention. The child finds another place to play.

events.title: A shared possession after separation
events.text: A household item was left between you and your former spouse. A relative asks you to settle who will keep it.

choices.text: Send it to your former spouse

outcomes.text: You send the item with the relative and ask for an acknowledgment that it arrived.

choices.text: Arrange a practical agreement

outcomes.text: You send a clear account of which items each household still needs. The relative helps carry the reply.

choices.text: Keep it set aside until you can agree

outcomes.text: You leave the item unused and separate from the rest of your things. The question remains open.

events.title: A customer wants a different pattern
events.text: A customer changes the painted pattern after you have prepared a group of clay vessels. The pieces have not yet been fired.

choices.text: Redo the pattern on the agreed pieces

outcomes.text: You remove the unfinished decoration and paint the new pattern. The extra work gives you more practice, but delays the batch.

choices.text: Make a sample before changing the batch

outcomes.text: You paint one sample and show it to the customer. You agree which details to keep before starting the rest.

choices.text: Offer the original pattern as agreed

outcomes.text: You show the original sample and explain what was agreed. The customer accepts it rather than wait for a new batch.

events.title: The board is not straight
events.text: A board prepared for a carved fitting has bent while drying. Cutting the planned shape now would leave a poor fit.

choices.text: Mark a smaller fitting that will fit the wood

outcomes.text: You change the layout and cut the smaller fitting. The customer needs fewer pieces than planned, but the fit is sound.

choices.text: Buy a replacement board for 5 drachmas

outcomes.text: You spend 5 drachmas on another board and keep the original measurements.

choices.text: Set it aside and explain the delay

outcomes.text: You explain why the board cannot be used as planned. The customer agrees to wait while you find suitable material.

events.title: A flaw in the stone
events.text: A dark line appears as you cut a small stone relief. You cannot yet tell whether it is only on the surface.

choices.text: Stop and check the line with another worker

outcomes.text: You check the surface together and alter the shallow cut. The flaw stays outside the main detail.

choices.text: Simplify the design around the flaw

outcomes.text: You redraw the border and explain the change to the customer before cutting farther.

choices.text: Set the piece aside for a later job

outcomes.text: You put the flawed piece aside and tell the customer you need another stone. The job remains unfinished.

events.title: A gap in the original
events.text: The text you are copying has an unreadable word. Guessing would make the finished copy look complete, but might change its meaning.

choices.text: Mark the gap clearly

outcomes.text: You leave a clear mark for the missing word. The recipient knows exactly where the original was unreadable.

choices.text: Ask to compare another copy

outcomes.text: Another copy preserves the missing word. You check it carefully and finish the line.

choices.text: Ask the owner how they want the gap handled

outcomes.text: You show the damaged line to the owner and agree how to mark it in the finished copy.

events.title: A learner disagrees
events.text: A learner challenges the example you used in a discussion. They can explain why it does not fit their experience.

choices.text: Work through their objection

outcomes.text: You ask them to explain each step, then revise the example together. The discussion lasts longer than the lesson you planned.

choices.text: Ask the group to compare two examples

outcomes.text: The learners compare the examples and identify where each one breaks down.

choices.text: Leave the question for the next lesson

outcomes.text: You write down the objection and return to the remaining material. You will need a better example next time.

events.title: Cloud hides the observation
events.text: Cloud covers the part of the sky you planned to observe. There is still an earlier table to check indoors.

choices.text: Check the arithmetic in the earlier table

outcomes.text: You compare the entries and recalculate a short section. One copied number needs correction.

choices.text: Record that the observation was not made

outcomes.text: You mark the missed observation clearly rather than entering an estimate as if you had seen it.

choices.text: Put the work away for the night

outcomes.text: You cover the working sheet and leave the observation for another clear night.

events.title: A rope is too short
events.text: A rope prepared for a shore task does not reach the intended fastening. The crew asks how to rearrange the work.

choices.text: Move the load before fastening it

outcomes.text: The crew shifts the load to a position the rope can reach. You check the new arrangement before the work continues.

choices.text: Find a suitable replacement rope

outcomes.text: You fetch another rope and check its length before bringing it back. The task starts later, with the planned arrangement.

choices.text: Wait for the experienced crew to decide

outcomes.text: You keep the area clear while the experienced crew changes the arrangement.

events.title: A younger worker asks for advice
events.text: A younger worker asks how you handled a routine problem. You have time to show them, talk it through or leave it for another day.

choices.text: Demonstrate the task slowly

outcomes.text: You show each step and let the younger worker repeat it. They get the last part right without another prompt.

choices.text: Explain how to check their own work

outcomes.text: You point out the signs of a mistake and ask them to inspect their attempt. The correction is theirs to make.

choices.text: Suggest asking again on a quieter day

outcomes.text: You explain that you cannot give the task enough attention today. They agree to return another time.

events.title: Things kept for years
events.text: You are sorting household possessions and find several small tools nobody has used for years.

choices.text: Pass a few on to someone who can use them

outcomes.text: You give the unused tools to someone who needs them and keep the ones still useful at home.

choices.text: Explain each tool and sort them by use

outcomes.text: You show the household what each tool does. The useful pieces are put where someone can find them.

choices.text: Wrap them and put them back

outcomes.text: You wrap the tools to keep them dry and put them back in storage. There is more room after the rest is sorted.

endings.title: Death in infancy
endings.text: You die before your first birthday. Your household arranges your funeral.

endings.title: Death in childhood
endings.text: You die during childhood. Your household arranges your funeral.

endings.title: Death in adulthood
endings.text: You die as an adult. Your household arranges your funeral and deals with your unfinished work.

endings.title: Death in later life
endings.text: You die in later life. Your household arranges your funeral and sorts your belongings.

endings.title: Record complete
endings.text: The record stops at age 100. This is the end of the simulation record, not a recorded death.

endings.title: Killed by a collector
endings.text: A collector stabs you during a confrontation over the unpaid loan. The chest wound proves fatal.

sources.title: Strabo, Geography 17.1.3–10: the Nile and Alexandria
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; H. L. Jones, Loeb translation (1932)
sources.period: Augustan-era account of Egypt and Alexandria, referring also to earlier Ptolemaic history
sources.summary: Describes Alexandria's harbors, Pharos, streets and royal district, and the importance of Nile inundation, canals and agricultural management.
sources.limitations: Elite literary testimony with Roman imperial sympathies. Descriptive claims and reported numbers are not a population survey, an exact city map or annual household probabilities.

sources.title: Bellum Alexandrinum 1–33: the Alexandrian War
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; Loeb translation (1955)
sources.period: Events of 48–47 BCE; authorship traditionally associated with the Caesarian corpus
sources.summary: Narrates fighting, barricades, harbor operations and disruption of Caesar's water supply during the Alexandrian War.
sources.limitations: A partisan Roman military narrative with prejudicial descriptions of Alexandrians. It supports a war setting, not invented civilian experiences, precise casualty odds or a claim that the entire Library was destroyed.

sources.title: Chronological Tables for Caesar's Wars (58–45 BCE)
sources.publisher: John T. Ramsey and Kurt A. Raaflaub, Histos 11 (2017); journal page published online 2018
sources.period: 58–45 BCE, including the Alexandrian War of 48–47 BCE
sources.geography: Roman campaigns including Alexandria and Egypt
sources.summary: Reconstructs the sequence of Caesar's campaigns and separates Roman civil-calendar dates from reconstructed Julian dates.
sources.limitations: A scholarly chronology reconstructed from ancient testimony. Day-level dates may be disputed; the game uses year-level anchors and does not reproduce whole tables.

sources.title: Ptolemaic Period
sources.publisher: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities
sources.period: 332–30 BCE; Actium in 31 BCE and the end of Ptolemaic rule in 30 BCE
sources.summary: Provides a heritage-authority overview of Ptolemaic Egypt and the transition following the defeat at Actium.
sources.limitations: A broad public-history overview, not a detailed social dataset. Use the year-level chronology without treating its compressed narrative as proof of every personal consequence.

sources.title: Augustus, Res Gestae, especially section 27
sources.publisher: Livius.org; F. W. Shipley translation from LacusCurtius
sources.period: Augustus's retrospective inscription, completed near the end of his reign in 14 CE
sources.geography: Roman Empire; section 27 concerns annexation of Egypt
sources.summary: Augustus claims to have added Egypt to Roman rule. The inscription offers a contemporary imperial voice for the political transition.
sources.limitations: Self-promotional imperial testimony. It does not describe the response of all Egyptians and must be paired with independent chronology and local evidence.

sources.title: Alexandrian Documents from the Reign of Augustus
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, Department of Classics, University of Cincinnati
sources.period: Augustan Alexandria, especially 13 BCE; individual texts and later additions have their own dates
sources.geography: Documents issued in Alexandria, many recovered from reused cartonnage at Abusir el-Melek
sources.summary: Provides scholarly English translations of Alexandrian contracts, letters, petitions and association records, with document identifiers and links to the underlying Greek texts.
sources.limitations: The surviving archive is selective, not representative of every household. Early Roman material is comparative evidence for earlier Ptolemaic years; use each document's actual date.

sources.title: BGU 4.1125.1–15: apprenticeship contract for a musician
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: March/April 13 BCE
sources.summary: Records training in flute playing, the term of apprenticeship, provision of food and clothing, and examination by fellow practitioners.
sources.limitations: The apprentice is enslaved, and this is a specific musical contract. It is evidence for organized training, not universal schooling or the terms of a free child's scribal apprenticeship.

sources.title: BGU 4.1058: wetnursing contract
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: 30 March 13 BCE
sources.summary: Documents paid nursing, infant care and a clause anticipating the possibility of a child's death.
sources.limitations: Both nurse and infant are enslaved in this contract. Its clauses show contemporary concerns; they do not estimate infant mortality or demonstrate that every household employed a wet nurse.

sources.title: BGU 4.1052.1–34: marriage contract
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: 15 April 13 BCE
sources.summary: Records an agreement for a shared life, a dowry and economic and marital obligations.
sources.limitations: One Greek-language legal agreement, with particular status and guardianship conventions. Its terms are not universal Egyptian marriage rules or an observed marriage-age distribution.

sources.title: BGU 4.1141: private letter
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: After 9 April 13 BCE
sources.summary: Preserves correspondence concerning friendship, accusations, work, wages and interpersonal obligations.
sources.limitations: A fragmentary and sometimes difficult personal letter, embedded in unequal relationships. It supports written communication as a theme, not the fictional character's letter or a literacy rate.

sources.title: BGU 4.1117: lease contract for a bakery
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: April/May 13 BCE
sources.summary: Describes a bakery lease, equipment, rent, repairs and responsibility for taxes, illustrating workshop livelihoods and contractual obligations.
sources.limitations: A single bakery agreement. Monetary amounts and conditions cannot be generalized to all trades or converted directly into the game's abstract wealth score.

sources.title: BGU 4.1151.1–18: partial payment of an inheritance
sources.publisher: Peter van Minnen, University of Cincinnati, translation of the primary papyrus
sources.period: 12 April 13 BCE
sources.summary: Records an agreement concerning the partial payment of an inheritance, supporting a narrative theme of property and obligations between generations.
sources.limitations: A particular legal settlement. It supplies neither a representative inheritance amount nor evidence that all older people held transferable property.

sources.title: Education and Apprenticeship
sources.publisher: Nikolaos Lazaridis (2010), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
sources.period: Survey across ancient Egyptian periods, including Ptolemaic and Roman bilingual education
sources.summary: Reviews training for scribes and specialist crafts, educational exercises and restricted access to formal schooling.
sources.limitations: A long-period synthesis with uneven evidence. It cannot supply exact Alexandrian enrolment or literacy probabilities, and does not justify giving every child formal schooling.

sources.title: Funerary Rituals (Ptolemaic and Roman Periods)
sources.publisher: Christina Riggs (2010), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology; University of East Anglia repository
sources.period: Ptolemaic and Roman periods
sources.geography: Egypt; evidence includes Akhmim, Thebes, Tuna el-Gebel and other communities
sources.summary: Surveys burial, commemoration, mourning and funerary associations, including arrangements for members to contribute to funeral costs.
sources.limitations: Rites varied with community, status, resources and religion. Elite mummification evidence is not a universal Alexandrian funeral script; use broad remembrance themes carefully.

sources.title: The abuse of aged parents in the ancient Roman world
sources.publisher: Tim Parkin, Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies 66(2), 41–50; online 2024
sources.period: Roman world with Ptolemaic Egyptian petitions of 225 and 221 BCE among the comparative cases
sources.geography: Roman Mediterranean and the Arsinoite nome in Egypt
sources.summary: Examines duties, dependence and care between generations, including papyrus petitions by older parents.
sources.limitations: Sparse, often one-sided dispute evidence from varied times and places. It does not establish rates of neglect or a uniform old-age household arrangement in Alexandria.

sources.title: Volcanic suppression of Nile summer flooding triggers revolt and constrains interstate conflict in ancient Egypt
sources.publisher: Joseph G. Manning and colleagues (2017), Nature Communications 8, 900; author copy at UC Berkeley
sources.period: Ptolemaic Egypt, 305–30 BCE, with later Nilometer measurements used for comparison
sources.geography: Nile basin and Egypt; papyrus survival particularly strong in the Fayyum
sources.summary: Combines environmental reconstructions and ancient writings to examine Nile flood variability, agricultural vulnerability and social stress.
sources.limitations: Ancient flood indications are intermittent and may have dating uncertainty. The continuous Nilometer series begins in 622 CE; this is not a precise annual Alexandrian food-price or famine-risk dataset.

sources.title: Roman Model Life Table (Coale–Demeny Female West Level 3)
sources.publisher: Columbia University / W. V. Harris teaching resources
sources.period: Comparative Roman demographic model; not an observed Ptolemaic cohort
sources.geography: Roman comparison model; not an Alexandria-specific dataset
sources.summary: Provides age-band mortality, survivorship and remaining life expectancy for a model population with life expectancy at birth of 25 years.
sources.limitations: A female model life table, not measured male Alexandrian rates. Converting interval death probabilities into annual hazards assumes within-band timing. Age at death is simulated, not a historical prediction.

sources.title: Quantifying antiquity
sources.publisher: Roger S. Bagnall, Columbia University
sources.period: Contrasts Roman Egyptian census evidence with Hellenistic Egyptian household lists
sources.summary: Explains the promise and limits of ancient demographic evidence, including why Hellenistic household lists without ages cannot yield life expectancy.
sources.limitations: A methodological essay rather than a downloadable life table. It explicitly cautions against combining Roman and Hellenistic evidence without careful analysis.

sources.title: Life Expectancy
sources.publisher: Sonia Zakrzewski (2015), UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
sources.period: Long-period review of ancient Egyptian demographic evidence, including Roman model tables
sources.geography: Egypt; evidence from varied populations and sites
sources.summary: Explains demographic methods and biases. Table 1 reproduces a model life table for Roman Egyptian females after Bagnall and Frier (1994), with life expectancy at birth of 22.5 years.
sources.limitations: A later-period female model inferred using census returns and Coale–Demeny West, not observed mortality for a male in Ptolemaic Alexandria. Annual interpolation and the final age-band policy are additional game assumptions; cause-of-death rates are not supplied.

sources.title: Zodiaque de Dendéra (E 13482)
sources.publisher: Musée du Louvre, Egyptian Antiquities collection
sources.period: 50 BCE; catalogue dates the relief to June–August
sources.summary: Catalogues a sandstone ceiling relief with zodiacal signs, decans and constellations, providing a contemporary example of Egyptian astral imagery.
sources.limitations: A temple object from Dendera, not an Alexandrian teaching manual. It supplies neither access probabilities nor evidence that astrological predictions were reliable.

sources.title: Alexandrian terracottas
sources.publisher: Vatican Museums, Gregorian Egyptian Museum
sources.period: Ptolemaic and Roman periods
sources.geography: Alexandria; collection objects have varied acquisition histories
sources.summary: Describes Alexandrian figurative terracottas, including mould-made examples and a range of decorative and religious subjects.
sources.limitations: The collection spans multiple periods and some objects entered through the antiquities market. It does not measure workshop employment, wages or apprenticeship access.

sources.title: Statuette of an ancestral king (2003.154)
sources.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.period: Late Period–Early Ptolemaic Period, 380–246 BCE
sources.geography: Egypt; exact workshop not established in this catalogue entry
sources.summary: Documents a carved wooden ritual figure associated with temple equipment, illustrating skilled Egyptian wood carving.
sources.limitations: Earlier than the player's lifetime and not specifically Alexandrian. The object's interpretation is debated; it does not establish a universal carving curriculum or job ladder.

sources.title: An enigmatic early horoscope: BKT X 29 (P. 11831)
sources.publisher: Berlin Papyrus Database, Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection; Marius Gerhardt, Andreas Winkler and Michael Zellmann-Rohrer
sources.period: Late Ptolemaic or early Roman handwriting; astronomical reconstruction best fits 5 June 29 BCE
sources.summary: Examines a Greek horoscope listing astral positions, abbreviations, the ascendant and midheaven, with possible professional or client use.
sources.limitations: The papyrus lacks a personal name and explicit date, and its solar position conflicts with the proposed reconstruction. Its use is uncertain, and no accompanying interpretation survives.

sources.title: Plutarch, Life of Antony 80: Areius and Octavian at Alexandria
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb translation
sources.period: Later biography describing the Roman takeover of Alexandria in 30 BCE
sources.summary: Depicts the philosopher Areius receiving public favour from Octavian and interceding for others, illustrating elite intellectual patronage and political access.
sources.limitations: A retrospective literary account, not an administrative record or promotion dataset. It concerns an exceptional elite figure and does not prove ordinary access to Cleopatra's court.

sources.title: Coins in Egypt: Coins of the Ptolemies
sources.publisher: University College London, Digital Egypt for Universities
sources.period: Ptolemaic Egypt, with an overview of earlier coinage
sources.summary: Introduces Ptolemaic coin circulation, drachma denominations, bronze and silver coinage, and debt settlement as part of the economy.
sources.limitations: An overview of money and denominations, not an Alexandrian household budget or price series. It does not support the game's prices, wages, asset valuations, fixed returns or a constant currency standard across Roman rule; these remain disclosed gameplay assumptions.

sources.title: LGPN-Egypt: personal names in Egypt
sources.publisher: University of Oxford, Lexicon of Greek Personal Names
sources.period: Current completed coverage: Lower Egypt and the Fayum from the seventh century BCE to 30 BCE; the wider project extends into Roman Egypt
sources.geography: Egypt, with current database coverage focused on Lower Egypt and the Fayum
sources.summary: Introduces a source-based naming database that records personal names alongside attested occupations, dates, family connections and provenance. It supports a varied Greek-language and Egyptian-rendered naming context for fictional characters.
sources.limitations: The game does not reproduce database individuals or claim that every selected name is attested in Alexandria in 66 BCE. Names are not demographic weights, ethnic labels, gender rules or evidence that an occupation belonged to a particular community. Household profiles and event rewards remain authored fiction.

sources.title: Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 1.81.7: childhood learning and livelihood
sources.publisher: LacusCurtius, University of Chicago; C. H. Oldfather, Loeb translation (1933)
sources.period: First-century BCE literary account of Egyptian customs
sources.geography: Egypt generally; not an Alexandrian household survey
sources.summary: Describes children learning livelihood skills from fathers and relatives, alongside limited and uneven access to literacy instruction.
sources.limitations: A generalizing literary account without numerical starting ages. It supports learning and work overlapping in childhood, not the game's exact age gates, wage amounts, universal schooling or an identical experience across households.

sources.title: BGU 4.1124: cancellation of a nailsmith's apprenticeship
sources.publisher: University of Cincinnati, Ancient Alexandria documentary translations
sources.period: After June/July 18 BCE, under early Roman rule
sources.summary: Records Hermaiskos, a son not yet of age, being trained in nailsmithing; cancelling the agreement permits his father to place him with another master.
sources.limitations: The apprentice's numerical age is unstated. The document postdates the cohort's Ptolemaic childhood and does not establish age 12 as a norm, free access to an apprenticeship or the game's pay and skill gains.

sources.title: BGU 4.1151.2: Loan agreement
sources.publisher: University of Cincinnati; Peter van Minnen translation
sources.period: 12 April 13 BCE, early Roman period
sources.summary: Records a money loan with scheduled instalments, default penalties and enforcement claims against debtors and workshop property.
sources.limitations: One early Roman contract, later than the Ptolemaic beginning of the game. Contractual enforcement clauses do not establish how frequently they were exercised or support violent collectors, murder, or the game's loan terms and risks.

economy.description: Household accounts use drachmas (dr). Net worth includes cash and the estimated sale value of possessions, less debt. Unpaid unavoidable costs can become debt. Amounts are fixed game values, not reconstructed historical prices or wages. There is no modern-currency conversion or automatic interest. The same simplified unit continues after Roman rule. A voluntarily accepted moneylender loan has its own balance and deadline. Ordinary household debt keeps automatic repayment; this loan must be paid deliberately. Its upfront charge and optional extension charge are fixed game terms, not measured ancient prices. Collectors pursue only that accepted loan.

assets.title: Workshop share
assets.description: Earn 10 drachmas each year you survive. Sell for 120 drachmas.

health.description: Early life keeps the easier health rules. From age 18, serious illness episodes use the full age-specific baseline from a Roman Egyptian female life-table comparison. Illness appears, Health falls and a care choice interrupts time before the condition can become fatal. Current Health, care and household support can change the outcome; dangerous choices retain their stated risks. Exact mortality for Ptolemaic Alexandria is unknown. The later Roman comparison is an estimate for the setting, not a measured rate for this character. Disease selection, severity and care effects are authored game rules.

relationships.description: Each introduced partner and born child has an individual closeness score. Contact can improve it, conflict can reduce it and prolonged neglect slowly erodes it. Close household members can help with recovery. These values and their effects are authored gameplay, not historical relationship measurements.

knowledge.description: Knowledge needs continued use. From age 12, two full years without a recorded learning gain lead to a loss of 1 point per year. Lessons, research, work and events with positive Knowledge effects refresh practice, including at the stat cap. Ageing also reduces Knowledge by 0.5 per year from 50, 1 from 65 and 1.5 from 80. These are authored game rules, not measured cognitive ageing rates. Skill proficiencies are separate.
